THE CONTROL IS CAPACITY- AND SAMPLE-MATCHED. A0 is the shipped architecture on the identical slice, run with train_filter set to the SAME finite-anchor mask, so it is not handed the ~20% of training episodes that inner block 1 costs A1. An unmatched A0 would make the residual arm look worse for a reason that has nothing to do with the residual.
PRIMARY: paired PER-EPISODE moving-block bootstrap on QLIKE(A0) - QLIKE(A1) over the pooled H=6 test slice, block max(round(n^(1/3)), 2H) = the existing block_len_for. Positive = A1 better. FAMILY SIZE 1, fixed now: one arm, one horizon. The twelve-cell family was spent on the QLIKE primary in P2-armA-result and this is a different measurement, not a thirteenth cell of that one.
SECONDARY, REQUIRED, R39: A1 must also beat the TEACHER on this slice both raw and with the teacher's own calib-fitted scalar c = sqrt(mean(RV^2/sigma^2)). A baseline denied a correction the candidate effectively has is not a baseline.
GUARDS, ALL MUST PASS, taken verbatim from P2-scale-v2: (i) calibration ratio mean(RV^2/sigma^2) in [0.95, 1.05]; (ii) neither the spike slice (RV >= 95th pct) nor the calm slice degrades by more than 2% relative; (iii) DSC not worse; (iv) Brier not worse. pinball, CRPS, logs and MCB are reported and their direction recorded whether or not they gate.
VERDICT RULE: ADOPTABLE requires the primary CI to exclude zero favourably AND every guard to pass AND the secondary to hold. Anything else is NOT ADOPTABLE, and a QLIKE gain alongside a failed guard is recorded as exactly that -- P2-scale-v2 is the precedent and R45 the rule. If this fails, the mechanism tag `teacher-residual` takes a strike under the stagnation rule.
experiments.result: pre-registered, not yet run
experiments.implication:
EXPECTED OUTCOME, RECORDED BEFORE THE RUN so it cannot be fitted afterwards.
I expect the primary to CLEAR and at least one guard to FAIL, and I expect the failing guard to be MCB or DSC rather than the calibration ratio. Reasoning: P2-armA-result decomposed the H=6 gain and found the constant part NEGATIVE (-68% of the total, implied c = 0.979), so unlike the scale correction this arm is not moving the level much and the calibration ratio should stay near where A0 leaves it. What the arm DOES do is hand the level to a low-variance linear estimator and leave the network only the deviation -- which makes the final sigma LESS responsive episode to episode, and DSC is precisely the measure of how much a forecast moves with the outcome. A smoother sigma is a better mean forecast and a worse discriminator, and that trade is invisible to QLIKE.
If instead DSC IMPROVES, my model of the mechanism is wrong: it would mean the residual network spends its capacity on conditional shape once the level is taken off its hands, which is the optimistic reading of the decomposition and the one that would justify Arm B.
If the primary does NOT clear in the shipped pipeline while it cleared in Arm A's own loop, the difference is the pipeline -- the H=19 committee calibration, the blend, Stage B -- and that would be the more important finding of the two, because it would mean Arm A's entire QLIKE table describes an estimator the product does not contain.

experiments.question: Does Arm A's H=6 QLIKE gain survive the barrier battery when the residual architecture runs through the SHIPPED pipeline?
experiments.rule:
AMENDMENT 1, recorded BEFORE THE HARNESS RUNS AND BEFORE ANY NUMBER EXISTS. Everything in P2-armA-adopt stands except the anchor VALIDATION, which as written was unsatisfiable by construction and would have voided the run for the wrong reason.
WHAT I HAD SEEN WHEN I WROTE THE AMENDMENT: no result. Only the two tables' shapes. teacher_oof.npz is built on episodes_h4, whose horizons are {1,6,24,168}; run_fold trains on the main episodes table, whose horizons are {6,12,19,24}. har_short is an OLS POOLED ACROSS HORIZONS, so fitting it on those two different training slices gives different coefficients and therefore different H=6 predictions. Demanding agreement to 1e-9 was demanding that two different fits coincide. That is a defect in my pre-registration, not evidence about Arm A.
REPLACEMENT VALIDATION, still a pass condition: on the pooled H=6 test slice the refitted anchor must (a) score within 2% relative QLIKE of teacher_oof.npz's har_short, and (b) correlate with it at Pearson r >= 0.98 in the log-vol domain. Both numbers are printed whether or not they pass. This establishes 'the same teacher in substance', which is what the gate actually needs; the identity check was asking for 'the same arithmetic', which the two tables make impossible.
Nothing about the primary, the control, the secondary, the guards, the family size or the verdict rule changes.
experiments.result: pre-registered, not yet run
experiments.implication:
The expected outcome recorded in P2-armA-adopt stands verbatim and is not restated here, so that the amendment cannot be read as an opportunity to revise the prediction.
ONE THING THE AMENDMENT ADDS. If the refitted anchor scores MATERIALLY BETTER than the artifact's har_short at H=6, that is itself a finding and not a convenience: it would mean the teacher's quality depends on which horizons it was pooled over, and every Phase 2 number that treats 'har_short' as one fixed object would need that caveat attached.

experiments.question: Does har_short's accuracy at a given horizon depend on WHICH horizons it was pooled over during fitting?
experiments.rule:
PRE-REGISTERED BEFORE THE ISOLATION RUNS. WHAT I HAD ALREADY SEEN, stated so this is not mistaken for a blind test: P2-armA-adopt-a1's anchor validation refused to score and printed the reason. har_short refitted on the MAIN episodes table (horizons {6,12,19,24}) scores QLIKE 0.37951 on the 49,124 shared H=6 test episodes, against 0.41710 for teacher_oof.npz's har_short, fitted on episodes_h4 (horizons {1,6,24,168}). That is -9.01%, and the artifact number 0.41710 is the same har_short P2-armA-result measured Arm A against.
WHAT IS NOT YET ESTABLISHED, and is the whole question: whether the difference is the HORIZON COMPOSITION of the training panel or something else about the two tables. har_short's five regressors -- har_1h, har_6h, har_1d, har_5d, har_22d -- are all ANCHOR features and do not vary with H (verified earlier: the columns that vary with H at a fixed anchor are seas_1d, seas_5d, seas_22d, cal_H, cal_weekend_frac). So at a given anchor the same x is paired with a different y = log(RV_H) - 0.5*log(H) for every H in the panel, and adding H=168 rows changes the fitted coefficients. That is the mechanism this experiment tests.
DESIGN. On episodes_h4 ALONE, so the table is held fixed and only the panel varies. Per walk-forward fold, fit har_short on the TRAIN slice restricted to each horizon panel, predict the H=6 TEST slice, pool. Panels: {1,6,24,168} (the artifact's), {6,24}, {6} alone, and {1,6,24} (drops only the long horizon). The main table's own {6,12,19,24} fit is reported alongside as the observation that prompted this, and is NOT one of the four panels, because it changes the table as well as the panel and so cannot isolate anything.
PRIMARY: pooled QLIKE at H=6 across folds, and the paired per-episode moving-block CI of {6}-alone minus {1,6,24,168}, block max(round(n^(1/3)), 12). FAMILY SIZE 3, fixed now: three alternative panels against the artifact's.
SECOND HORIZON, MANDATORY: the same four panels scored at H=24. One horizon could be a coincidence of which rows happen to dominate the fit; if the effect is pooling it should appear at both. FAMILY becomes 6 and the Bonferroni divisor is 6.
DECISION RULE. If a narrower panel beats {1,6,24,168} with a CI excluding zero at BOTH horizons, then every Phase 1 and Phase 2 number computed against a horizon-pooled baseline is measured against an UNDER-SPECIFIED baseline, and that must be stated wherever those numbers appear -- including the Phase 1 conclusion that har_short beats NOCTUA, which would become a conclusion about a WEAKER har_short than the one available. If the narrower panels do NOT beat it, the -9.01% is a property of the two tables rather than of pooling, and the anchor validation failure needs a different explanation before P2-armA-adopt can be re-run.
experiments.result: pre-registered, not yet run
experiments.implication:
EXPECTED OUTCOME, RECORDED BEFORE THE RUN. I expect the {6}-alone panel to win at H=6 and the {1,6,24,168} panel to be the worst of the four at both horizons, with the damage coming mostly from H=168: an OLS in the log hourly vol RATE domain is being asked to fit the same five trailing-vol regressors against a one-week target whose mean reversion is almost complete and a one-hour target whose is barely started, and the compromise coefficients serve neither.
IF I AM RIGHT, THE UNCOMFORTABLE PART IS NOT THE BASELINE. It is that NOCTUA is pooled over horizons too, by the same argument and with far more parameters, and nothing in this project has ever tested whether ITS pooling is costing it more than the baseline's costs the baseline. That would be the obvious next experiment and it is not this one.
IF I AM WRONG and the panels score alike, the -9.01% is about the tables, and the most likely cause is the finite-row mask: episodes_h4 keeps H=168 rows for which seas_1d and seas_5d are undefined, and any row-completeness rule that differs between the two tables changes which episodes the fit sees.

experiments.question: Does har_short's accuracy at a given horizon depend on WHICH horizons it was pooled over during fitting?
experiments.rule:
AMENDMENT 1. TWO CORRECTIONS AND ONE ADDITION, and I state exactly what I had seen when I wrote each, because two of them were prompted by numbers.
CORRECTION A -- A MISLABELLED REFERENCE, not a rule change. P2-pool-composition called the {1,6,24,168} panel 'the artifact's'. It is not. Reading eval/teacher_zoo.py's _fit_predict_fold shows the OOF artifact fits every OLS teacher PER HORIZON -- 'PER-HORIZON fits. Phase 1 established that a baseline fitted on a pooled multi-horizon sample is a straw man at the extremes (R39)' is the comment on the line. So the artifact's panel is `{H} alone`, which was already one of the four declared panels. The contrast the experiment contains is therefore the right one; only the reference column was misnamed, and the decision rule now reads against `{H} alone`. This is R41 again: the label I gave a panel was not a description of what was in it.
CORRECTION B -- A DEFECT IN THE FIRST RUN, found and fixed before any panel was interpreted. The completeness mask was built over all 42 feature columns. No H=168 row has a complete 42-column record (seas_1d and seas_5d read past the anchor once H > 24d), so the mask deleted the entire long horizon and the {1,6,24,168} panel silently became {1,6,24}. The mask is now the 40-column one teacher_zoo itself uses. The defective run is discarded; its reference number was 0.42905, which the corrected run reproduces exactly as the {1,6,24} panel -- which is the proof that the defect was what I said it was.
ADDITION -- THE RESCALE CONTROL, MANDATORY, added BEFORE it is run. WHAT I HAD SEEN: two rows of the H=6 table. {1,6,24,168} scores 0.38328 and {1,6,24} scores 0.42905, a paired -11.94% with CI [-0.06272, -0.03426]. I have NOT seen the {6,24} panel, the `{H} alone` panel, or anything at H=24.
WHY IT IS MANDATORY. QLIKE is asymmetric and is minimised by the conditional MEAN of variance, while an OLS in logs exponentiates to something below it. Changing which horizons enter the fit moves the INTERCEPT, and a panel that happens to sit at a higher level scores better for a reason that carries no information. This project has already rejected exactly that: garch_normal's spike and deep-tail wins at all four horizons were level bias, and rescaling destroyed them (P2-mechanism). A pooling comparison without the rescale control would be the same mistake with a different name.
THE CONTROL. Each panel additionally gets its OWN calib-fitted scalar, c = sqrt(mean(RV^2/sigma^2)) fitted PER FOLD on that fold's calib slice only -- per fold because R44 was written after a pooled-calib constant had to be withdrawn. Both the raw and the rescaled table are reported. THE VERDICT IS TAKEN FROM THE RESCALED TABLE. If a panel's advantage survives rescaling it is information about the conditional shape; if it does not, the finding is 'pooling moves the level' and the correct response is to fix the level, not to change the panel.
Family size, horizons and everything else are unchanged.
experiments.result: amended, re-running
experiments.implication:
MY PRE-REGISTERED PREDICTION IS ALREADY IN TROUBLE AND I AM RECORDING THAT NOW. I predicted 'the {6}-alone panel to win at H=6 and the {1,6,24,168} panel to be the worst of the four at both horizons, with the damage coming mostly from H=168'. The first two rows point the other way: adding H=168 to {1,6,24} IMPROVED H=6 by 11.94%. If that survives the rescale control then my account of the mechanism was backwards -- the long horizon is not distorting the fit, it is anchoring the level -- and the more likely reading is that the wide panel shrinks the short-window coefficients toward something more stable out of sample.
THE STAKES IF IT SURVIVES. The per-horizon fit was adopted deliberately, to stop the baseline being a straw man at the extremes. If it is worse in the middle, then every Phase 1 and Phase 2 comparison used a har_short weaker than the one available -- and since har_short already beats NOCTUA at three horizons, a stronger har_short makes NOCTUA's position worse, not better. That is the direction that matters and it is the uncomfortable one.
THE STAKES IF IT DOES NOT SURVIVE. Then this is one more instance of the single mechanism that has explained more Phase 2 results than anything else -- QLIKE rewarding a higher forecast level -- and the right conclusion is that the project should stop discovering it one experiment at a time and put the rescale control in front of every vol comparison by default.

experiments.question: Does the teacher ranking survive giving every teacher its own calib-fitted level scalar?
experiments.rule:
PRE-REGISTERED BEFORE THE RUN. WHAT I HAD ALREADY SEEN, stated so this is not mistaken for a blind test. P2-pool-composition's rescale control at H=6: har_short fitted per horizon scores 0.41710 raw and 0.35623 once it carries its own per-fold calib-fitted c (c = 1.171 to 1.219 across folds). The pooled-panel variants score 0.38255-0.38328 raw -- an 8% advantage -- and 0.35480 rescaled, +0.40% with CI [-0.00265, +0.00580], which does not clear. So the panel effect was level, and the level correction is worth 15% at H=6 while the panel choice is worth nothing.
WHY THAT PUTS THE SCORECARD IN QUESTION. teacher_scorecard.json ranks teachers by RAW pooled QLIKE and reports each one's calibration ratio beside it. Those ratios are not close to 1 and not close to each other: at H=6 they run from 0.8606 (garch_normal) to 1.4642 (noctua_v1), with har_short at 1.3930 and garch_t at 1.0514. A ratio of 1.05 against a ratio of 1.39 is a 13% level advantage to garch_t before any conditional information is compared, and garch_t is the declared winner at H=1 and H=6. The same arithmetic that made the wide panel look 8% better than the narrow one is available to explain the whole ranking.
DESIGN. No training. Read teacher_oof.npz. For every horizon and every teacher, fit c = sqrt(mean(RV^2/sigma^2)) on that fold's CALIB slice ONLY and apply it to that fold's TEST slice -- per fold, through FoldScopedFit, because a constant fitted on calib pooled across folds had to be withdrawn once already (R44). Report the raw ranking and the rescaled ranking side by side at all four horizons, on pooled, spike, calm and deep-tail, with the calibration ratio after rescaling as the check that the correction did what it claims.
PRIMARY, AND IT IS A RANKING QUESTION NOT A SUPERIORITY QUESTION: does the identity of the best teacher change at any horizon when every teacher is rescaled? Reported as a table, not a single test. Where a rank changes, the paired per-episode moving-block CI between the new winner and the old one is reported, block max(round(n^(1/3)), 2H). FAMILY SIZE 4, fixed now: one rank-change contrast per horizon. Failed cells stay in the family.
MANDATORY CONTROL, because this is the same trap one level up: the rescaling constant must be fitted on CALIB and only calib. A c fitted on test would make every teacher's calibration ratio exactly 1 by construction and the comparison would be meaningless. The reported post-rescale ratio is computed on TEST and is expected to be near but not exactly 1; a value of exactly 1.0000 is evidence the fit leaked and the run is void.
WHAT THIS DOES NOT LICENCE. Nothing about adoption. P2-scale-v2 established that applying a level correction to the shipped model improves QLIKE by 9.7% and degrades all six barrier metrics, so a rescaled ranking is a statement about which teacher carries more CONDITIONAL information, not a proposal to ship any of them rescaled.
experiments.result: pre-registered, not yet run
experiments.implication:
EXPECTED OUTCOME, RECORDED BEFORE THE RUN.
I expect the ranking to change at H=6 and H=1 and to hold at H=24 and H=168. At H=6 har_short goes from 0.41710 to 0.35623, which is already better than garch_t's RAW 0.41246, and garch_t starts at a ratio of 1.0514 so it has almost nothing left to gain -- I expect har_short to take H=6 outright. At H=1 har_short's ratio is 2.0343, the worst in the table, so it has the most to gain there too, but it starts from 1.03094 against garch_t's 0.57438 and I do not expect a scalar to close a gap that size; my guess is garch_t holds H=1 and the gap narrows. At H=168 the ratios are already 1.05 and the correction should change almost nothing.
IF I AM RIGHT ABOUT H=6, TWO PHASE 2 CONCLUSIONS MOVE. First, the calib-best teacher at H=6 was selected on raw calib QLIKE, where har_short scored 1.4015 with a calibration ratio of 2.4167 -- a selection made almost entirely on level. Second, and this is the one that costs something: P2-armA-result's surviving cell was H=6, where A1 scored 0.39020 and was declared to beat the calib-best teacher both raw and rescaled. Against a RESCALED har_short at 0.35623 it does not, and R39 entitles the baseline to that correction. If that holds, Arm A has no surviving cell and the residual architecture is rejected -- which is the outcome I would least like and the one this experiment exists to be capable of producing.
THE STRUCTURAL LESSON EITHER WAY. Three separate Phase 2 findings -- garch_normal's spike wins, the scale falsifier's c, and now the pooling panel -- have all reduced to forecast level. If the scorecard reduces to it as well, then the project has been running a level competition and calling it a teacher competition, and every future vol comparison should carry the rescale control by default rather than discovering it again.

experiments.question: Does har_short's accuracy at a given horizon depend on WHICH horizons it was pooled over during fitting?
experiments.rule: As pre-registered in P2-pool-composition and amended once before the run. The verdict comes from the RESCALED table; the raw table is reported in full beside it.
experiments.result:
THE PANEL EFFECT IS ENTIRELY LEVEL. Table is episodes_h4 throughout; the reference is the artifact's own panel, `{H} alone`, which the reconstruction reproduces to five decimals at both horizons (0.41710 at H=6, 0.27818 at H=24) -- that agreement is what licenses reading anything else in the table.
H=6, RAW:      {H} alone 0.41710 | {1,6,24,168} 0.38328 +8.11% CI [+0.02559,+0.04341] CLEARS | {6,24} 0.38255 +8.28% CI [+0.02568,+0.04670] CLEARS | {1,6,24} 0.42905 -2.86%.
H=6, RESCALED: {H} alone 0.35623 (c = 1.171-1.219) | {1,6,24,168} 0.35480 +0.40% CI [-0.00265,+0.00580] | {1,6,24} 0.35737 -0.32% CI [-0.00835,+0.00289] | {6,24} 0.35482 +0.40% CI [-0.00324,+0.00849]. NOTHING CLEARS. An 8.11% raw advantage becomes 0.40% and indistinguishable from zero.
H=24, RAW:     {H} alone 0.27818 | {1,6,24,168} 0.31555 -13.43% | {6,24} 0.31722 -14.03% | {1,6,24} 0.39683 -42.65%. The sign is OPPOSITE to H=6, which is itself the tell.
H=24, RESCALED: {H} alone 0.25696 | {1,6,24,168} 0.26182 -1.89% | {6,24} 0.26415 -2.80% | {1,6,24} 0.27801 -8.19%. The 42.65% collapses to 8.19% and the 13.43% to 1.89%.
MAIN TABLE, the observation that prompted all of this: har_short fitted on {6,12,19,24} scores 0.37951 raw at H=6 against the artifact's 0.41710, and 0.35589 rescaled against 0.35623. Nine percent apart raw; 0.1% apart once each carries its own scalar. Their log-vol correlation was already 0.9978.
TWO DEFECTS FOUND AND FIXED BEFORE INTERPRETATION, both recorded in the amendment. The completeness mask deleted every H=168 row and turned the widest panel into {1,6,24}; the corrected run reproduces the defective run's 0.42905 exactly as the {1,6,24} row, which is what proves the diagnosis (R47). And the panel labelled 'the artifact's' was not the artifact's -- teacher_zoo fits per horizon (R41, R46).
experiments.implication:
MY PRE-REGISTERED PREDICTION WAS WRONG IN DIRECTION AND WRONG IN MECHANISM, and the pre-registration is what makes that visible. I predicted the {6}-alone panel would WIN at H=6 and that the wide panel would be worst at both horizons, with the damage coming from H=168 distorting the fit. Raw, the wide panel won at H=6 by 8% and lost at H=24 by 13% -- and rescaled, no panel differs from any other. There was never a fitting-panel effect to explain; there was a level effect that changed sign with the horizon.
WHAT THE PER-HORIZON DECISION ACTUALLY BOUGHT. It was adopted so the baseline would not be a straw man at the extremes (R39). On this evidence it neither helped nor hurt once level is controlled, which means it was neither the improvement it was taken for nor the mistake this experiment was opened to investigate. It stays, on the grounds that it is the more defensible specification and costs nothing.
THE FINDING THAT MATTERS IS NOT ABOUT PANELS. This is the FOURTH Phase 2 result to reduce to forecast level -- after garch_normal's spike wins, the scale falsifier's constant, and the 9% anchor discrepancy that opened this. A comparison of two volatility forecasts under QLIKE is a comparison of their levels until proven otherwise, and this project has now proven it otherwise four times by accident. The rescale control belongs in front of every vol comparison by default, and P2-scorecard-rescaled applies it to the one comparison that has never had it: the teacher ranking itself.
experiments.lesson: THE 9% DISCREPANCY LOOKED LIKE A BUG IN MY RECONSTRUCTION AND WAS A PROPERTY OF THE METRIC. It arrived through a pre-registered validation that refused to let a run proceed, and the cheapest response would have been to relax the tolerance and carry on. The expensive response -- stop, reproduce the artifact exactly, then vary one thing -- cost about an hour and turned a blocked adoption test into the observation that reframed the phase.

experiments.question: Does the teacher ranking survive giving every teacher its own calib-fitted level scalar?
experiments.rule: As pre-registered, applied verbatim. c fitted on CALIB per fold through FoldScopedFit; the post-rescale ratio is computed on TEST and the run voids itself if any ratio is exactly 1.
experiments.result:
THE RANKING CHANGES AT THREE OF FOUR HORIZONS, AND THE NEW WINNER IS NOCTUA V1. Leak check passed: post-rescale TEST ratios run 0.9784-1.1389, none exactly 1.
H=1    raw garch_t 0.57438 -> rescaled noctua_v1 0.54985 beats garch_t 0.57235 by +0.02250 CI [+0.00427, +0.03774] CLEARS. RANK CHANGED.
H=6    raw garch_t 0.41246 -> rescaled noctua_v1 0.34884 beats garch_t 0.41073 by +0.06188 CI [+0.04145, +0.07837] CLEARS. Rescaled har_short is 0.35623, also beaten. RANK CHANGED.
H=24   raw har_short 0.27818 -> rescaled noctua_v1 0.25087 against har_short 0.25696, +0.00609 CI [-0.00183, +0.01231] DOES NOT CLEAR. Rank changes but the contrast is a tie.
H=168  har_short holds, raw 0.18207 and rescaled 0.18231; noctua_v1 0.19575. RANK HELD.
THE CAUSE IS ONE NUMBER PER TEACHER. NOCTUA has the WORST calibration ratio in the zoo at every horizon -- 1.4330 / 1.4642 / 1.4569 / 1.1660 -- meaning it under-forecasts variance by about 20% in sigma, consistently. Its fitted c is 1.198 / 1.212 / 1.213 / 1.089 and the rescale is worth 11.70% / 19.06% / 23.62% / 4.83% to it, more than to any other arm except the two GARCHs at H=168 where they are broken outright. garch_t starts at a ratio of 1.0174 and 1.0514 and has essentially nothing to gain: +0.35% and +0.42%. THE RAW RANKING WAS MEASURING WHICH ARM HAPPENED TO SIT AT THE RIGHT LEVEL.
MY PRE-REGISTERED PREDICTION WAS HALF RIGHT AND MISSED THE POINT ENTIRELY. I predicted har_short would take H=6 and garch_t would hold H=1. har_short does overtake garch_t at H=6 (0.35623 vs 0.41073) exactly as predicted -- and both are beaten by NOCTUA, which I did not consider at all because I was reasoning about the two teachers whose numbers I had in front of me.
experiments.implication:
THE PHASE 1 DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG AND THE PHASE 1 CONCLUSION WAS RIGHT, AND KEEPING THOSE APART IS THE WHOLE POINT. Phase 1 concluded that NOCTUA does not beat a properly specified HAR family at any horizon. AS A STATEMENT ABOUT THE SHIPPED FORECAST THAT STANDS: raw is what ships, and raw it loses at H=6, 24 and 168. What is now falsified is the DIAGNOSIS attached to it -- that NOCTUA lacks something the HAR family has. It does not. Once the level is equalised NOCTUA carries MORE conditional information than every teacher in the zoo at H=1 and H=6, ties the best at H=24, and only genuinely loses at H=168.
THIS DOES NOT LICENCE ADOPTING THE RESCALE, AND THAT IS NOT A TECHNICALITY. P2-scale-v2 ran exactly that adoption test: QLIKE improved 9.7% pooled and 33% on spikes, the calibration ratio went 1.2662 -> 0.9759, and ALL SIX barrier metrics degraded -- DSC -14.16%, MCB +8.48%, Brier, CRPS, log score and pinball. The product is a touch-probability curve, not a sigma. So the finding is a REDIRECTION, not a change: the binding constraint on NOCTUA is a single stable level bias, and the naive correction for it breaks the thing the model is for.
WHAT THIS KILLS. The premise of Phase 2 was that stronger models must become teachers because har_short and garch_t beat NOCTUA. On conditional information they do not. Teacher mining aimed at importing what the HAR family knows is aimed at a gap that does not exist, and Arms B and C -- OOF stacking and a gated MoE over these same teachers -- inherit that premise. They should not be built until the level question is settled.
WHAT THIS COSTS ARM A. Its surviving cell was H=6, where A1 scored 0.39020 and was recorded as beating the calib-best teacher raw and rescaled. Against a rescaled har_short at 0.35623 and a rescaled NOCTUA at 0.34884 it does neither, and R39 entitles both to that correction. Arm A has no surviving cell once its comparators are equipped, and the barrier battery it was queued for is now measuring the wrong question.
THE REAL QUESTION, WHICH IS NOW THE ONLY ONE WORTH ASKING: why is a strictly proper quantile-trained network biased 20% low in level, stably, across six years and four horizons -- and can that be fixed at the TRAINING objective, where Stage B and the committee would inherit a correctly levelled sigma, instead of by a post-hoc multiplier that they cannot absorb? A post-hoc scalar shifts a recorded median. A training-time fix changes what the quantiles mean. P2-scale-v2 tested the first and it failed; nothing has tested the second.
experiments.lesson: I HAVE NOW DISCOVERED THE SAME MECHANISM FOUR TIMES UNDER FOUR NAMES -- garch_normal's spike wins, the scale falsifier's constant, the pooling panel, and the teacher ranking -- because the rescale control was run as a response to a suspicion each time instead of as a default. A control that has overturned four results in one phase is not a control, it is part of the metric. Every future QLIKE comparison in this project reports raw and rescaled side by side, and the burden is on the raw number to explain itself.

experiments.question: Is NOCTUA's level bias exactly the median-vs-mean gap, and does the model's OWN per-episode conversion survive the barrier battery that a constant failed?
experiments.rule:
PRE-REGISTERED BEFORE THE HARNESS EXISTS. WHAT I HAD SEEN, in full, because this experiment was suggested by numbers rather than by theory:
  (a) P2-scorecard-rescaled: NOCTUA's calibration ratio is the worst in the zoo at every horizon (1.4330 / 1.4642 / 1.4569 / 1.1660) and its fitted scalar is c = 1.198 / 1.212 / 1.213 / 1.089. Equalise level and it is the best teacher in the zoo at H=1 and H=6.
  (b) noctua/infer.py ALREADY returns `sigma_mean` beside `sigma_med`, built from the model's own atom grid as sqrt(mean(exp(2*atoms_y))*H), and its docstring records that the mean/median ratio is 1.205.
  (c) 1.205 against a fitted 1.198-1.213 is agreement to about half a percent at three horizons. If that is not coincidence, the level bias IS the median-vs-mean gap, the model already computes the correction from its own predicted quantiles, and the correction is per-episode and has ZERO fitted parameters.
  (d) The same docstring asserts the mean 'scores worse'. That assertion is not accompanied by a run, and it is inconsistent with (a) -- a factor of 1.205 is within half a percent of the fitted optimum, so it cannot score worse on QLIKE unless the per-episode variation is actively harmful. R34: a comment saying a thing was checked is not a check. It is treated here as a hypothesis to test, not as evidence.
SLICE. The PRODUCTION slice, H=19, identical to P2-scale-v2, so every barrier number is directly comparable to the ones that failed there. Not a horizon chosen after the fact.
ARMS, all four declared now:
  M0  shipped, sigma_med. The reference.
  M1  sigma_mean: post_shift_fn returns the PER-EPISODE delta_i = log(sigma_mean_i /       sigma_med_i), so the corrected level reaches Stage B, the committee and every barrier       rather than re-weighting a recorded median.
  M2  THE CONSTANT, mandatory: delta = the mean of delta_i over that fold's CALIB slice only.       This is P2-scale-v2's correction re-derived from the model instead of fitted to the       target. It is in the family so that M1 is forced to show it does something the constant       does not. If M1 and M2 are indistinguishable, the per-episode variation is decoration.
  M3  THE CONTROL: delta_i permuted across episodes within the fold, preserving the marginal       distribution and the mean exactly while destroying the alignment with the episode. If       M3 matches M1, the gain is the mean shift and M1 falls with it.
TWO PASSES, and the reason it is exactly two. delta_i is read off the model's own prediction, so it is not available before the model runs. Pass A predicts with no shift and records sigma_mean/sigma_med on the calib and test slices; pass B re-runs with those deltas. The ratio is INVARIANT to the shift -- a uniform shift moves qa, the atoms and the median together -- so one iteration is exact rather than approximate, and run_fold's existing assertion that the achieved log-level shift equals the requested one to 1e-6 is retained as a pass condition.
IS delta_i FITTED ON TEST? No. It is a function of the model's own predictive distribution at that episode and uses no target. M2's constant, which does use targets through the calib mean, is fitted on CALIB and per fold (R44).
PRIMARY: paired per-episode moving-block bootstrap on QLIKE(M0) - QLIKE(M1) over the pooled production slice, block max(round(n^(1/3)), 2H). FAMILY SIZE 3, fixed now: M1, M2, M3 on one slice. Failed arms stay in the family.
GUARDS, taken verbatim from P2-scale-v2 because this is the same adoption question with a different correction: (i) calibration ratio in [0.95, 1.05]; (ii) neither spike nor calm degrades more than 2% relative; (iii) DSC not worse; (iv) Brier not worse. pinball, CRPS, logs and MCB are reported with their direction whether or not they gate.
VERDICT RULE: M1 is ADOPTABLE only if the primary CI excludes zero favourably AND every guard passes AND M3 does NOT clear. If M1 clears and the guards fail in the same pattern as P2-scale-v2 -- QLIKE up, all six barriers down -- then the barrier degradation is a property of moving the level AT ALL and not of how the shift was obtained, and that closes the level question in the other direction: the correction has to change what the QUANTILES mean during training, not shift them afterwards. Either outcome is worth the run.
experiments.result: pre-registered, not yet run
experiments.implication:
EXPECTED OUTCOME, RECORDED BEFORE THE RUN.
I expect M1 to clear the primary by roughly what P2-scale-v2's constant did -- 9 to 10% pooled -- and I expect the barrier guards to FAIL, in the same direction and for the same reason. My argument: a touch probability is set by where the barrier sits in the predictive distribution, and raising the whole distribution raises every touch probability. The CORP decomposition then charges that as miscalibration (MCB up) and the isotonic recalibration removes most of the benefit, leaving DSC roughly flat or down. Nothing about deriving the shift from the model's own quantiles rather than fitting it changes that geometry.
WHERE I COULD BE WRONG, AND IT IS THE INTERESTING CASE. delta_i is not constant -- it is large exactly where the model's predicted distribution is WIDE, which is where it is least certain. A correction that lifts the level more in uncertain episodes and less in confident ones is a genuinely conditional operation, and DSC measures exactly whether a forecast moves with the outcome. If M1's DSC IMPROVES while M2's degrades, the per-episode variation is carrying real information and the median-vs-mean conversion is the first level correction in this project that is not a level correction. That is the outcome M3 exists to keep me honest about.
IF M1 AND M2 ARE INDISTINGUISHABLE the answer is clean and negative: the spread of delta_i is too small to matter, the whole thing is the 1.205 constant, and P2-scale-v2 has already answered it. In that case the level question moves to the training objective and the next experiment is a loss-function change, not a post-hoc one.

experiments.question: Does Arm A's H=6 cell survive comparators that are equipped under R39?
experiments.rule:
No new experiment. This entry applies R39 -- a baseline denied a correction the candidate effectively has is not a baseline -- to numbers that already exist, and records the consequence for P2-armA-result. P2-armA-result is immutable and is superseded, not edited.
The comparators come from P2-scorecard-rescaled, which gives every teacher its own per-fold calib-fitted scalar. That is the same correction Arm A's own pre-registration already required of the teacher -- 'A1 ... BEATS the calib-best teacher garch_t both raw (0.41246) and rescaled (0.41073)' -- applied to ALL the comparators instead of only to the one that calib had selected.
experiments.result:
ARM A HAS NO SURVIVING CELL. At H=6, A1 scored 0.39020. The comparators, all on the same 49,124 test episodes:
  garch_t rescaled   0.41073   A1 beats it, as P2-armA-result reported
  har_short rescaled 0.35623   A1 LOSES by 9.5%
  noctua_v1 rescaled 0.34884   A1 LOSES by 11.9%
P2-armA-result compared A1 only against the CALIB-SELECTED teacher, garch_t. That selection was itself made on raw calib QLIKE, where har_short scored 1.4015 with a calibration ratio of 2.4167 -- so garch_t was chosen over har_short on level, and then A1 was declared a winner against the arm that level selection had produced.
The other three cells are unchanged and were already failures: H=1 A1 is worse than A0 from scratch; H=24 beat raw har_short and not rescaled har_short, which P2-armA-result had already recorded as not a win; H=168 did not clear.
THE DECOMPOSITION RESULT SURVIVES AND IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING. A3, teacher-as-feature, cleared at ZERO horizons and was significantly worse than its teacher at H=1, exactly as pre-registered -- 'a feature column can be ignored or diluted by the network while an additive offset cannot'. That is a statement about inductive bias and it does not depend on which comparator the arms were scored against.
P2-armA-adopt is CLOSED WITHOUT RUNNING. The barrier battery was queued to ask whether A1's H=6 QLIKE gain survives into the product metrics. There is no gain to carry: the arm loses to two properly equipped comparators on the metric it was supposed to have won. Running the battery would consume six folds of training to characterise a rejected arm.
experiments.implication:
THE MECHANISM TAG `teacher-residual` TAKES ITS FIRST STRIKE under the stagnation supervisor. Two more failed architecture changes built on it and it is closed.
THE HARNESS IS KEPT AND IS NOT WASTED. `benchmark.run_fold(residual_anchor=...)` routes any additive anchor through Stage B, the committee and every barrier, with the achieved-shift assertion intact. That is the general mechanism for testing ANY decomposition through the product metrics rather than beside them, and the level work now in front of it needs exactly that path. The anchor validation that refused the run is kept for the same reason.
WHAT I GOT WRONG, PRECISELY. Not the experiment -- the pre-registration was specific, the controls were real, the decomposition prediction about A3 was sharp and it held. What I got wrong was accepting `calib-best teacher` as the definition of the bar without asking what calib was ranking on. TEACHER_ZOO section 5 says preserve disagreement between metrics rather than collapsing everything into one score; the calibration ratio WAS in the scorecard, in the column next to the one I selected on, reading 2.4167 against 1.0035. I read the ranking and not the column beside it.
experiments.lesson: A SELECTION RULE INHERITS EVERY BIAS OF THE METRIC IT SELECTS ON. 'Best by calibration QLIKE' was written to avoid selecting on test, which it did. It did not avoid selecting on level, and nothing in the protocol asked it to. When a scorecard prints a diagnostic beside the ranking column -- here, a calibration ratio spanning 0.83 to 2.42 -- the ranking is a hypothesis about that diagnostic until the diagnostic is controlled.

experiments.question: Is NOCTUA's level bias exactly the median-vs-mean gap, and does the model's OWN per-episode conversion survive the barrier battery that a constant failed?
experiments.rule:
AMENDMENT 1, recorded WHILE THE RUN IS IN FLIGHT AND BEFORE ANY OF ITS NUMBERS EXIST. Nothing in the design, the arms, the guards, the family size or the verdict rule changes. What is added is a cross-reference I should have made before writing the prediction, drawn entirely from artifacts that already existed when I wrote it.
THE NUMBER I HAD NOT PUT NEXT TO THE OTHERS. scale_adopt.json records the per-fold optimal scalar ON THE PRODUCTION SLICE, H=19: 1.130 / 1.163 / 1.114 / 1.171 / 1.142 / 1.107, mean about 1.138. The scorecard's optimal scalars are horizon-dependent -- 1.198 / 1.212 / 1.213 at H=1, 6, 24 and 1.089 at H=168 -- and H=19 sits between the last two, so 1.138 is exactly where it should be.
THE MODEL'S OWN RATIO IS NOT HORIZON-DEPENDENT IN THE SAME WAY. infer.py records sigma_mean/sigma_med as roughly 1.205 regardless. So on THIS slice the model's own conversion is expected to OVERSHOOT the optimum by about 6%, which would drive the calibration ratio from 1.2662 to roughly 1.2662/1.205^2 = 0.87 -- outside the pre-registered guard band [0.95, 1.05] on the low side, i.e. over-forecasting.
WHY THE SLICE IS NOT CHANGED. H=19 was chosen so every barrier number is directly comparable to the ones that failed in P2-scale-v2. Moving the slice after noticing the overshoot would be choosing the horizon where the answer is nicest, which is the thing pre-registration exists to prevent. The run stands as specified.
experiments.result: running
experiments.implication:
THE PREDICTION IN P2-mean-level STANDS VERBATIM AND IS NOT REVISED. I predicted M1 clears the primary by roughly 9-10% and fails the barrier guards. On the cross-reference above I now think it may also fail the RATIO guard by over-correcting, and I am recording that as a SECOND, LATER, WEAKER prediction rather than replacing the first -- so that if M1 does clear cleanly, the record shows I had two chances to be right and used both.
WHAT THE MISMATCH WOULD MEAN IF IT HOLDS. The correction the model needs varies with horizon -- 1.21 at a day, 1.09 at a week -- and the correction the model DERIVES from its own quantiles does not. That is a statement about the predicted DISPERSION: if the level bias were purely the lognormal median-to-mean gap, the model's own spread would carry the horizon dependence automatically, because the conditional spread of log RV genuinely narrows as the averaging window lengthens. It apparently does not, which would mean the network's predicted quantile spread is too flat across horizons -- a defect in the shape of the predictive distribution rather than in its centre, and a different problem from the one this experiment was opened to test.
THAT WOULD BE THE MOST USEFUL OUTCOME AVAILABLE, because it is testable directly and cheaply: compare the model's predicted log-vol spread against the realized conditional spread, per horizon, on data that already exists.

experiments.question: Can the adaptive correction that SHIPS remove the level bias that P2-scorecard-rescaled measured?
experiments.rule: No new experiment and no new fit. Two ratios computed from teacher_oof.npz, which is frozen, on NOCTUA V1's own cross-fitted test-slice forecasts. Both are the standard summaries of the same forecast/outcome pairs, so any disagreement between them is a statement about which functional each one targets and nothing else.
experiments.result:
THE SHIPPED CORRECTION TARGETS THE WRONG FUNCTIONAL AND CANNOT REMOVE THIS BIAS.
`serve/adaptive.py` computes factor = MEDIAN(realized / sigma_med) over a trailing 60-day window of settled episodes, clipped to [0.70, 1.40], and `apply_correction` multiplies sigma_atoms and sigma_med by it. The QLIKE-relevant scalar is sqrt(mean(RV^2 / sigma^2)). On NOCTUA's own OOF test predictions:
   H     median(RV/sigma)   sqrt(mean(RV^2/sigma^2))   frac(RV < sigma)   n
   1        0.8864                 1.1971                 0.6047        49,123
   6        0.9958                 1.2100                 0.5051        49,124
  24        1.0540                 1.2070                 0.4195        49,106
 168        0.9358                 1.0798                 0.5979        48,962
The median ratio is 0.89-1.05 -- near 1, which is what a correctly calibrated MEDIAN forecast should give, and frac(RV < sigma) sits near 0.5 at H=6 confirming it. The QLIKE scalar is 1.08-1.21 at the same time on the same episodes. The two disagree because they are different functionals of the same conditional distribution, and only one of them is the one QLIKE is minimised by.
AT H=1 THE SHIPPED CORRECTION POINTS THE WRONG WAY. Its factor there would be 0.886 -- it would LOWER a forecast that the QLIKE scalar says is 20% too low, making the loss worse rather than better.
AND IT MOVES THE BARRIERS WHILE DOING IT. apply_correction scales sigma_atoms, which is the conditioning input to every touch probability. That is precisely the operation P2-scale-v2 measured end to end: QLIKE +9.7%, and all six barrier metrics degraded.
experiments.implication:
THIS IS A PRODUCTION FINDING, NOT A RESEARCH ONE, AND IT IS THE FIRST THING IN THIS PHASE THAT IS ACTIONABLE WITHOUT A TRADE-OFF. The adaptive correction is not wrong to exist -- a trailing check that the forecast has not drifted is a genuine safety mechanism, and near 1 is the right answer for the quantity it measures. It is wrong to have been expected to fix the level bias, and nothing in the repository claimed it would; the two were simply never put side by side.
IT ALSO EXPLAINS WHY THE BIAS SURVIVED. A monitor reading 0.9958 at H=6 says 'the median forecast is calibrated', which is TRUE, and reads as 'the forecast is calibrated', which is false under QLIKE. The instrument was working and was answering a different question than the one anyone was asking of it.
THE NARROW FIX IS OBVIOUS AND THE BROAD ONE IS NOT. sigma_med and the touch-probability curve are TWO PRODUCTS with different losses: QLIKE on a variance point forecast wants the conditional MEAN; the barrier curve is scored by proper rules on the predictive DISTRIBUTION, which the level correction should not touch at all. serve/predict.py already reads them from different places -- `sigma_window_pct` from pred['sigma_med'], the curves from model.touch_prob(pred, ...) -- so correcting the reported sigma without touching the predictive object is a one-line change whose barrier metrics are identical to the shipped ones BY CONSTRUCTION. That is P2-level-report and it is pre-registered separately.
experiments.lesson: A CALIBRATION MONITOR IS ONLY A MONITOR FOR THE FUNCTIONAL IT MEASURES. This one measured the median ratio, reported ~1.0 for years, and was structurally incapable of seeing a 20% bias in the mean. When a model reports one functional and is scored on another, every diagnostic in between has to declare which of the two it is watching.

experiments.question: Does reporting the conditional-MEAN volatility, while leaving the predictive object untouched, fix the QLIKE level bias at no cost to the barrier curves?
experiments.rule:
PRE-REGISTERED BEFORE THE HARNESS EXISTS. WHAT I HAD SEEN: P2-scorecard-rescaled (NOCTUA's QLIKE scalar is 1.198/1.212/1.213/1.089), P2-scale-v2-result (applying a scalar THROUGH the pipeline improves QLIKE 9.7% and degrades all six barrier metrics), and P2-adaptive-wrong-functional (the shipped monitor watches the median ratio, which is 0.89-1.05 on the same episodes). P2-mean-level is still running and none of its numbers are in.
THE IDEA, STATED PLAINLY SO IT CAN BE ATTACKED. sigma and the touch-probability curve are TWO PRODUCTS scored by DIFFERENT losses. QLIKE on a variance point forecast is minimised by the conditional MEAN. The barrier curve is scored by strictly proper rules on the predictive DISTRIBUTION, and P2-scale-v2 measured that moving that distribution's level degrades every one of them. So the correction belongs to the REPORTED FUNCTIONAL and not to the distribution. serve/predict.py already reads them from different places -- sigma_window_pct from pred['sigma_med'], the curves from model.touch_prob(pred, ...) -- so the change is confined by the existing structure rather than by an argument.
ARMS, on the PRODUCTION slice H=19, one predictive object per fold and three READINGS of it:
  R0  sigma_med, the shipped reading. Reference.
  R1  sigma_mean, already computed by infer.py from the model's own atom grid. PER EPISODE,       ZERO fitted parameters.
  R2  c * sigma_med with c = sqrt(mean(RV^2/sigma^2)) fitted on that fold's CALIB slice only       (R44). One fitted parameter, and the ceiling R1 is trying to reach without fitting.
PRIMARY: paired per-episode moving-block bootstrap on QLIKE(R0) - QLIKE(R1), block max(round(n^(1/3)), 2H). FAMILY SIZE 2, fixed now: R1 and R2 on one slice.
GUARD ON THE CALIBRATION RATIO: the reported sigma's mean(RV^2/sigma^2) must land in [0.95, 1.05]. R1 has no free parameter and may overshoot -- P2-mean-level-a1 records, before either run, that the model's own mean/median factor is about 1.205-1.246 against an optimum near 1.138 on this slice -- and if it does, R1 fails this guard and R2 is the arm that stands.
THE VERIFICATION THAT MATTERS IS NOT A STATISTIC. 'The barriers are unchanged' is true by construction here, and a claim that cannot fail is not a claim (R2). So the pass condition is a SERVING REGRESSION TEST: run serve/predict.py against a fixed anchor before and after the reporting change and assert that every touch_prob, every safe_level, p_up and p_vol_amplify are BIT-IDENTICAL, and that exactly the two sigma fields moved. A test that would fail if the change leaked into the predictive object.
WHAT THIS IS NOT. It is not a model improvement. Nothing the model knows changes, no barrier gets sharper, and no arm in the teacher zoo is beaten by it that was not already beaten by the rescaled ranking. It is a correction to WHICH NUMBER IS PUBLISHED under a loss that names a different one, and it must be written up in exactly those terms. If the write-up cannot resist calling it a 9% improvement, it should not ship.
ADOPTION: allowed only with the primary clearing, the ratio guard passing for the arm being adopted, and the serving regression test green. The model artifact is NOT retrained and NOT modified; this touches the reporting layer only, which is what keeps it inside TEACHER_ZOO section 8's rule that the shipped model stays untouched during teacher discovery.
experiments.result: pre-registered, not yet run
experiments.implication:
EXPECTED OUTCOME, RECORDED BEFORE THE RUN. R2 clears comfortably -- it is the fitted optimum and P2-scale-v2 already measured that scalar's QLIKE gain at 9.7% on this slice, which is not in doubt; what was in doubt was whether the barriers survived, and here they cannot be touched. R1 clears the primary but FAILS the ratio guard by over-correcting, for the reason recorded in P2-mean-level-a1. So my prediction is: adopt R2, reject R1, and the honest headline is 'the published volatility number now matches the loss it is scored under'.
THE CASE AGAINST THIS WHOLE IDEA, WHICH I WANT ON THE RECORD BEFORE THE NUMBERS ARRIVE. A reader can reasonably say that publishing sqrt(E[RV^2]) instead of the median is choosing the estimator that flatters the metric, and that if the barrier curve is the real product then QLIKE was never the right scoreboard. I think the answer is that a variance-swap or implied-vol quote IS a square-root-of-mean-variance object, so the mean is the more correct thing to publish next to an IV number regardless of QLIKE -- but that is an argument about what the dashboard is for, not a measurement, and it should be labelled as such wherever this result appears.
IF R2 IS ADOPTED, ONE THING GETS WORSE AND IT SHOULD BE SAID: the reported sigma and the barrier curve will then be derived from DIFFERENT functionals of the same distribution, so a user who tries to reconstruct the touch probabilities from the published sigma with a lognormal assumption will not reproduce them. That is a documentation obligation, not a defect, and it is the price of scoring two products with two losses.

experiments.question: Is NOCTUA's level bias exactly the median-vs-mean gap, and does the model's OWN per-episode conversion survive the barrier battery that a constant failed?
experiments.rule: As pre-registered in P2-mean-level and amended once before the run. Guards verbatim from P2-scale-v2.
experiments.result:
NOT ADOPTABLE, and the reason is more general than the arm. Production slice, 2,046 test episodes, blocks of 38, Bonferroni family 3.
  arm                       QLIKE     vs M0     rel%    paired CI
  M0 shipped              0.29688         -        -    (reference)
  M1 per-episode delta    0.25326  +0.04362  +14.69%   [+0.01603, +0.07443]  CLEARS
  M2 constant             0.26506  +0.03182  +10.72%   [+0.00901, +0.05649]  clears
  M3 SHUFFLED CONTROL     0.27605  +0.02083   +7.02%   [-0.00284, +0.04680]  does not clear
  M1 vs M2                         +0.01180             [-0.00095, +0.02364]  NOT SEPARATED
THE BARRIER BATTERY DEGRADES IDENTICALLY UNDER ALL THREE ARMS:
  metric        M0        M1        M2        M3
  DSC     0.009104  0.007169  0.007544  0.007254   all worse, all about -20%
  MCB     0.024752  0.026985  0.027386  0.027395   all worse
  brier   0.180094  0.184262  0.184287  0.184587   all worse
  crps    0.005251  0.005484  0.005542  0.005543   all worse
  logs    0.527476  0.538441  0.538252  0.539145   all worse
  pinball 0.003577  0.003724  0.003756  0.003763   all worse
GUARDS: ratio_in_band FAIL (1.2656 -> 0.9120, overshoot into over-forecasting), dsc_not_worse FAIL, brier_not_worse FAIL; spike, calm and control_does_not_clear PASS; primary PASS.
THE MODEL'S OWN FACTOR IS NOT THE STABLE 1.205 THE DOCSTRING RECORDS. Per fold it is 1.2458 / 1.1362 / 1.2100 / 1.1769 / 1.1254 / 1.1227, mean 1.1686, against per-fold QLIKE optima of 1.1297 / 1.1625 / 1.1141 / 1.1715 / 1.1416 / 1.1069. It scatters around the target by +10.3% / -2.3% / +8.6% / +0.5% / -1.4% / +1.4% rather than sitting biased above it, and sd(delta) itself swings 0.0395 to 0.1272 between folds.
experiments.implication:
BOTH OF MY PRE-REGISTERED PREDICTIONS HELD, INCLUDING THE ONE I DID NOT WANT. I predicted M1 clears the primary by 9-10% and the barrier guards fail (it clears by 14.69% and they fail), and in the amendment I predicted the ratio guard fails by over-correcting (0.9120, out of band on the over-forecasting side). The optimistic branch I flagged -- 'if M1's DSC IMPROVES while M2's degrades, the per-episode variation is carrying real information' -- did not happen: M1 0.007169, M2 0.007544, M3 0.007254, all about -20% and indistinguishable.
THE CONTROL IS WHAT MAKES THIS DECISIVE, AND IT IS THE RESULT. M3 shifts the level by the SAME mean with the per-episode alignment destroyed. It degrades every barrier metric by essentially the same amount as M1 and M2. So THE BARRIER DAMAGE IS CAUSED BY MOVING THE LEVEL AT ALL, not by how the shift is obtained, not by fitting it to the target, and not by any property of the median-to-mean conversion. P2-scale-v2 found this with a fitted constant; this run shows a derived per-episode shift and a randomised shift do it identically. The level question is closed in that direction: no post-hoc shift applied through the predictive object can pass this battery.
WHAT THE PER-EPISODE VARIATION IS AND IS NOT WORTH. M1 beats M2 by +0.01180 with the CI straddling zero at the corrected level, so within this run it is not separated from the constant. It is worth noting -- not claiming -- that M1's 14.69% exceeds the 9.7% P2-scale-v2 got from the QLIKE-OPTIMAL constant on this same slice, while M1's calibration ratio is further from 1 than that constant's was. A shift that is worse on level and better on loss is a shift carrying conditional information. That is a cross-run comparison and it is labelled as one; the within-run contrast is the one that governs and it says not separated.
WHERE THE LEVEL WORK GOES NOW, and it was pre-registered before this ran: 'the correction has to change what the QUANTILES mean during training, not shift them afterwards.' Two live routes. (i) P2-level-report, already pre-registered and queued: sigma and the barrier curve are separate products with separate losses, so correct the REPORTED functional and never touch the predictive object -- by construction the barriers cannot move. (ii) A training-time objective change, which nothing has tested.
experiments.lesson:
I DID NOT STATE AN MDE FOR THIS RUN AND R5 REQUIRES IT. The primary is comfortably powered -- the observed effects are 10-15% against a production-slice pooled MDE recorded elsewhere at about 8.44% -- so the verdict is unaffected. The M1-vs-M2 contrast at +3.97 percentage points on 2,046 episodes is the one that needed the number in advance, and because I did not write it down I cannot now say whether 'not separated' means 'the same' or 'not resolvable here' without deciding it after seeing the interval. It is recorded as NOT SEPARATED and is not read as evidence of equality.
THE CONTROL EARNED ITS COST. M3 was three extra full pipeline runs per fold and it converted a second failed adoption test into a general statement about the barrier pipeline. Without it, the honest reading of M1 and M2 both failing would have been 'two corrections failed', not 'the pipeline rejects level corrections as a class'.

experiments.question: Does reporting the conditional-MEAN volatility, while leaving the predictive object untouched, fix the QLIKE level bias at no cost to the barrier curves?
experiments.rule: As pre-registered, applied verbatim. Family 2, Bonferroni. The offline gates are the primary CI and the calibration-ratio band; ADOPTION additionally requires the serving regression test, which is a separate deliverable and is not claimed here.
experiments.result:
R2 CLEARS BOTH OFFLINE GATES; R1 CLEARS THE PRIMARY AND FAILS THE RATIO GUARD. Production slice, 2,046 test episodes, blocks of 38.
  reading                    QLIKE      vs R0    rel%    ratio   paired CI
  R0 sigma_med (shipped)   0.29688          -       -   1.2656   (reference)
  R1 sigma_mean (no fit)   0.25326   +0.04362  +14.69   0.9120   [+0.01785, +0.07238]  OUT OF BAND
  R2 c*sigma_med (1 fit)   0.26806   +0.02882   +9.71   0.9761   [+0.01146, +0.04693]  in band
R2's +9.71% reproduces P2-scale-v2's 9.7% on the same slice with the same constant. The difference between the two experiments is not the number, it is that here the constant never enters the predictive object, so no barrier can move. R1's 0.25326 is bit-identical to P2-mean-level's M1, which cross-checks the post_shift_fn machinery: it landed the median exactly on sigma_mean.
THE PRODUCTION FINDING, MEASURED RATHER THAN QUOTED. serve/predict.py's comment says the raw forecast runs high and realized lands below it 66.4% of the time. On the production slice, same episodes, same run:
  median(RV/sigma)          0.9664   <- the factor serve/adaptive.py applies
  sqrt(mean(RV^2/sigma^2))  1.1250   <- the factor QLIKE is minimised by
  frac(RV < sigma)          0.5552
THE TWO POINT IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS. The shipped correction LOWERS the forecast by 3.4% while the loss it is scored under wants it RAISED by 12.5%. P2-adaptive-wrong-functional established that the monitor is blind to this bias; this measures that on the production slice it actively works against it.
MY PREDICTION HELD EXACTLY: 'adopt R2, reject R1'. R1's ratio of 0.9120 is out of band on the over-forecasting side, for the reason recorded in P2-mean-level-a1 -- the model's own mean/median factor averages 1.1684 against a fitted optimum of 1.1370.
experiments.implication:
WHAT IS NOT YET ESTABLISHED, AND IT IS THE ONLY THING THAT MATTERS FOR ADOPTION. The claim 'the barriers cannot move' is true by construction inside this harness, and a claim that cannot fail is not a claim (R2). The gate is a SERVING REGRESSION TEST: run forecast() with the reporting scalar forced to 1 and with the real scalar and assert every touch_prob, every safe_level, p_up and p_vol_amplify are bit-identical while exactly the two sigma fields moved. That test CAN fail -- it fails the moment the scalar leaks into the predictive object -- and until it is green R2 is ADVANCE, not ADOPT.
THE SERVING SCALAR IS NOT THE OFFLINE ONE AND THAT GAP NEEDS ITS OWN MEASUREMENT. Offline, c is fitted on a six-month calibration slice. At serving there is no fold, so it has to come from a trailing window of settled episodes -- and sqrt(mean(RV^2/sigma^2)) is a mean of squares, far more outlier-sensitive than the median the existing monitor uses. Whether a 60-day trailing estimate tracks the fold-fitted c is an empirical question that the offline artifacts can answer, and it must be answered before anything ships.
AND THE HONEST FRAMING, RESTATED BECAUSE IT IS EASY TO LOSE. This is not a model improvement. Nothing the model knows changes, no barrier gets sharper, and no teacher is newly beaten. It corrects WHICH NUMBER IS PUBLISHED under a loss that names a different one. The 9.71% is the size of a units error, not the size of a discovery.
experiments.lesson: THE SAME CORRECTION FAILED AND PASSED DEPENDING ONLY ON WHERE IT WAS APPLIED. P2-scale-v2 put c inside the predictive object and lost all six barrier metrics; P2-level-report puts the identical c on the reported number and loses nothing, because there is nothing downstream of it. Before asking whether a correction is right, ask which product it is a correction TO -- this project spent three phases treating one model as one product.

experiments.question: Can a TRAILING estimate of the QLIKE scalar do the job of the fold-fitted one at serving, and what does the shipped correction actually cost?
experiments.rule:
P2-level-report-result left one thing explicitly unestablished before anything could ship: 'Whether a 60-day trailing estimate tracks the fold-fitted c is an empirical question that the offline artifacts can answer, and it must be answered before anything ships.' This answers it, from level_report.npz, with no new training.
CAUSALITY. At episode i the estimator uses episodes [i-60, i) only. The production slice is one episode per day at 17:00 with H=19, so episode i-1 settles at 12:00 on the day of episode i's anchor -- every episode in the window has closed before the anchor it is used at. This is the same settled-window rule serve/adaptive.py's _settled_anchors already enforces.
FOUR SCALARS, SCORED ON THE SAME EPISODES: none, the fold-fitted c (the offline ceiling, not available at serving), the trailing QLIKE scalar sqrt(mean(RV^2/sigma^2)) over 60 settled episodes, and the TRAILING MEDIAN factor median(RV/sigma) -- which is what serve/adaptive.py computes and ships today.
experiments.result:
THE TRAILING SCALAR WORKS, AND THE SHIPPED CORRECTION IS WORSE THAN NOT CORRECTING AT ALL.
  QLIKE  sigma_med, uncorrected        0.29519
  QLIKE  x fold-fitted c               0.26733   the offline ceiling
  QLIKE  x TRAILING QLIKE scalar       0.26849   within 0.4% of the ceiling
  QLIKE  x trailing MEDIAN factor      0.31441   WHAT SHIPS TODAY -- 6.5% WORSE THAN DOING NOTHING
  calibration ratio under the trailing scalar: 1.0086, inside the [0.95, 1.05] guard.
The trailing QLIKE scalar has mean 1.1240, sd 0.0999, range [0.9098, 1.3960] over 2,046 episodes and NEVER leaves serve/adaptive.py's existing clip band [0.70, 1.40], so the existing safety rail needs no change. The trailing MEDIAN factor has mean 0.9645 and range [0.7737, 1.1228] -- it sits below 1 and lowers the forecast.
IT DOES NOT TRACK THE FOLD VALUE EPISODE BY EPISODE and does not need to: corr(trailing, fold c) = +0.018, mean absolute error 0.0848. Both simply live near 1.12-1.14, and the trailing one scores within 0.4% of a constant fitted with six months of hindsight. What matters for the loss is the level it sits at, not whether it anticipates the fold.
experiments.implication:
THIS UPGRADES P2-adaptive-wrong-functional FROM 'BLIND' TO 'HARMFUL', WITH A NUMBER. That entry established the shipped monitor watches the median ratio and therefore cannot see a bias in the mean. This measures what it does instead: it applies a factor of about 0.96, lowering a forecast the loss wants raised, and the corrected series scores 0.31441 against 0.29519 for leaving it alone. The correction is not a small miss in the right direction. It is a 6.5% loss for the privilege of being adjusted.
AND IT IS NOT AN ARGUMENT FOR REMOVING THE MONITOR. median(RV/sigma) near 1 is the correct reading for a calibrated MEDIAN forecast and is a genuine drift check -- if it ever moved to 0.7 that would be real news. The defect is that its output is multiplied into the forecast rather than reported as a health signal. Two different jobs, one number.
WHAT SHIPS, IF THE REGRESSION TEST IS GREEN: the trailing QLIKE scalar multiplies the REPORTED sigma only; the predictive object, and therefore every touch probability and safe level, is untouched; the median factor stays exactly where it is as a diagnostic. That is three separable changes and the ledger should be able to tell them apart afterwards.
experiments.lesson: THE CHEAPEST EXPERIMENT OF THE PHASE ANSWERED THE QUESTION THAT BLOCKED SHIPPING. It cost one numpy pass over an artifact that existed because a previous run was patched to dump its per-episode arrays. Writing those arrays out cost nothing and saved six folds of retraining.

experiments.question: Does the reporting fix pass its serving gate, and what exactly changed?
experiments.rule: P2-level-report's adoption condition, applied verbatim: the primary CI clears, the ratio guard passes for the arm adopted, and the SERVING REGRESSION TEST is green.
experiments.result:
ADOPTED, reporting layer only. The model artifact is not retrained and not modified.
SERVING GATE, tests/test_level_report.py, 5/5:
  scalar-applied                     trailing QLIKE scalar 1.1113 on live history
  only-sigma-moved                   fields that changed: sigma_annualized_pct, sigma_window_pct
  both-sigma-moved                   the reported sigma carries it
  sigma-moved-by-exactly-the-scalar  ratio 1.1113 against scalar 1.1113
  gate-can-fail                      a deliberately leaked scalar moves 18 barrier fields and
                                     the comparison sees it
The fifth check is the one that makes the other four mean anything (R2). Every touch probability, safe level, p_up and p_vol_amplify is bit-identical between the two runs.
THREE SEPARABLE CHANGES, so the record can tell them apart later:
  1. serve/adaptive.py gains `qlike_scale` -- same settled-episode window, same STRIDE_HOURS, same CLIP_LO/CLIP_HI rail, different functional.
  2. serve/predict.py multiplies the REPORTED sigma by it and nothing else, and publishes a `sigma_scale` block naming exactly which fields it applies to.
  3. The existing median-based `volatility_correction` and `apply_correction` are UNCHANGED and still applied to the predictive object. Its output simply stops being the thing that sets the published volatility number.
The rail was not widened: over 2,046 production episodes the trailing QLIKE scalar ran 0.9098 to 1.3960 and never left [0.70, 1.40]. CI gains the gate as a required step.
experiments.implication:
WHAT THIS IS WORTH, STATED THE WAY THE PRE-REGISTRATION DEMANDED. The published volatility number was 12.5% low against the loss it is scored under, and the correction that shipped made it 6.5% worse than doing nothing. That is a units error and a monitor pointed at the wrong functional -- not a discovery, not a better model, and not 9.71% of new skill. Nothing the model knows changed. No barrier got sharper. No teacher is newly beaten.
WHAT IS STILL OPEN AND IS NOW THE ONLY LEVEL QUESTION LEFT. The barrier curve is still built from a predictive distribution whose level is 12.5% low, and every post-hoc attempt to move that level has failed the barrier battery -- a fitted constant (P2-scale-v2), the model's own per-episode conversion, and a randomised shift, all degrading all six metrics by the same amount. The remaining route is the one nothing has tested: change what the quantiles mean during TRAINING, so Stage B and the committee are fitted at the corrected level rather than having it imposed after.
A DOCUMENTATION OBLIGATION FALLS OUT, and it was recorded before the run. The published sigma and the touch probabilities are now different functionals of the same distribution, so a user who assumes lognormality and reconstructs the curves from the published sigma will not reproduce them. The `applies_to` string in the payload says so at the point of use; the model card should say it too.
experiments.lesson: THE FIX WAS AVAILABLE FOR THE WHOLE PROJECT AND WAS INVISIBLE BECAUSE NOBODY ASKED WHICH PRODUCT THE CORRECTION BELONGED TO. infer.py has returned `sigma_mean` beside `sigma_med` from the beginning, with a docstring stating the median/mean gap and asserting the mean 'scores worse' -- an assertion with no run behind it that turned out to be right for the wrong reason (the mean overshoots) and to have discouraged the right question. Three phases of work treated one model as one product.

experiments.question: Can a richer hour-of-day basis capture the intraday error structure the single Fourier harmonic cannot represent?
experiments.rule: As pre-registered, applied verbatim. Family 8, Bonferroni. The shuffled-hour control must not clear. Barriers are not scored and NO ADOPTION FOLLOWS from this entry regardless of outcome.
experiments.result:
ONE CELL OF EIGHT CLEARS, AND IT IS THE ONE I PREDICTED COULD NOT. The control never clears, at any horizon.
  H     base      B1 (3 harmonics)            B2 (23 dummies)             shuf (CONTROL)
    1  0.72068   -0.35% [-0.00413,-0.00080]   -0.12% [-0.00244,+0.00126]  -1.86% [-0.01633,-0.01088]
    6  0.41360   -0.19% [-0.00271,+0.00119]   -0.12% [-0.00244,+0.00126]  -4.05% [-0.02078,-0.01344]
   24  0.27207   +0.35% [-0.00121,+0.00382]   +1.21% [+0.00047,+0.00722]  +0.02% [-0.00207,+0.00276]
  168  0.17410   -1.34% [-0.00856,+0.00497]   -0.66% [-0.00633,+0.00562]  -1.33% [-0.00866,+0.00472]
B2 at H=24 CLEARS at the corrected level, +1.21%, and B1 at H=1 is significantly WORSE. Everything else straddles zero.
THE CONTROL IS THE MEASUREMENT, AND ITS HORIZON PATTERN IS THE FINDING. 23 columns whose hour label is MEANINGLESS cost 1.86% at H=1, 4.05% at H=6, 0.02% at H=24 and 1.33% at H=168. The capacity penalty is not a constant -- it is large where the target is noisy and vanishes at H=24. Set the true labels against it: at H=1 the real basis costs 0.12% where the fake one costs 1.86%, at H=6 0.12% against 4.05%. THE CLOCK INFORMATION IS REAL AT EVERY HORIZON AND IT IS WORTH ALMOST EXACTLY THE CAPACITY IT CONSUMES -- and only at H=24, where the capacity is free, does any of it reach the bottom line.
The fold-level comparison was declared NOT POWERED before the run at an 18.89% MDE and is not reported as a measurement.
experiments.implication:
MY EXPECTED OUTCOME IS FALSIFIED, AND IN THE SHARPEST AVAILABLE WAY. I wrote: 'I expect a clear gain at H=1, a smaller one at H=6, and NOTHING at H=24 and H=168', reasoning that a 24-hour window contains every hour so the anchor hour cannot say which part of the day the forward window covers. The gain appears ONLY at H=24 and fails at both horizons where I said it would work. I also pre-registered the escape hatch -- 'if H=24 or H=168 DOES improve, my explanation is wrong and the gain is coming from something other than intraday timing, most likely raw capacity, which is exactly what the shuffled-hour control is there to detect' -- and the control REFUSES that explanation too: it clears nowhere and is flat at H=24. So the H=24 gain is neither the mechanism I proposed nor the artifact I named as its alternative.
ONE PREDICTION HELD: B2 beats B1 wherever they differ, +1.21% against +0.35% at H=24, which is what a sharp three-hour swing that three harmonics smooth over should look like.
THE POST-HOC EXPLANATION, LABELLED AS POST-HOC AND NOT TESTED HERE. The control's horizon profile tracks target noise: base QLIKE is 0.72 at H=1 and 0.27 at H=24, and the capacity penalty is 1.86% and 0.02% respectively. A noisier target makes 23 extra parameters more expensive, and the clock signal is too small to pay that price. If that is right, the information is recoverable at H=1 and H=6 by a basis that carries it with FEWER parameters -- and B1, at six columns, is not that test, because it also carries LESS of the signal. The clean version is a ONE-parameter feature targeting the measured block, an indicator for the 13:00-19:00 UTC window that P2-event-footprint located. That is a new experiment and it gets its own pre-registration; it is not run off the back of this one.
NO ADOPTION FOLLOWS, as the rule said before the run. Barriers were not scored, and P2-scale-v2-result established that a QLIKE gain on this model can coexist with across-the-board barrier degradation.
experiments.lesson: THE CONTROL ANSWERED A QUESTION THE PRIMARY COULD NOT ASK. It was put in to detect capacity masquerading as signal, which it did not find. What it found instead -- by having a value at every horizon rather than just a verdict -- is that the COST of capacity varies 200-fold across horizons and that variation, not the signal, explains the whole table. A control that only reports pass or fail throws that away.

experiments.question: Is the intraday error footprint sharper in US EASTERN local time than in UTC, as scheduled macro releases would require?
experiments.rule:
PRE-REGISTERED BEFORE THE MEASUREMENT. A diagnostic on data that already exists -- teacher_oof.npz, H=1 test slices, NOCTUA V1's own cross-fitted forecasts -- with no new training and no new feature.
THE HYPOTHESIS, AND WHY IT IS SHARP. Every US macro release and market open is scheduled in EASTERN LOCAL TIME and therefore moves by ONE HOUR IN UTC twice a year: 8:30 ET is 13:30 UTC in winter and 12:30 UTC in summer; the 9:30 ET equity open is 14:30 and 13:30; the 2:00 pm ET FOMC statement is 19:00 and 18:00. If scheduled releases drive the footprint, then measuring it in UTC must SPLIT each event across two adjacent hours, and measuring it in Eastern local time must merge each pair into one.
P2-event-footprint's UTC lift table is consistent with exactly that and I am recording the reading BEFORE testing it: the two largest lifts are ADJACENT (14:00 = 1.788, 13:00 = 1.201) and the second cluster is an ADJACENT PAIR (18:00 = 1.533, 19:00 = 1.465). Two doublets is what a DST-split schedule produces and is not what a genuine UTC-anchored effect would produce.
STATISTICS, FIXED NOW. (i) OMNIBUS: chi-square of the worst-5% hour distribution against the all-episode hour distribution, computed in UTC and in America/New_York. (ii) CONCENTRATION, the primary: the share of worst-5% episodes falling in the THREE highest-lift hours of each clock. If the Eastern clock merges the doublets, its top three hours must capture MORE of the worst 5% than UTC's top three do.
CONTROL, MANDATORY: the same statistics computed on clocks shifted by a FIXED offset of every integer 1..23 hours from UTC. A fixed offset cannot merge a DST doublet -- it moves both halves together -- so no fixed-offset clock should beat the Eastern one on concentration. If some fixed offset beats it, the effect is not daylight saving and the Eastern reading is a coincidence. This control is what separates 'the schedule is in Eastern time' from 'the peak happens to sit near a bin edge in UTC'.
SECOND CONTROL: the same measurement at H=24, where P2-event-footprint measured chi-square 3.0 and p = 1.000. Neither clock may show structure there. Structure at H=24 would mean the estimator is finding something other than intraday timing.
WHAT THIS MAY AND MAY NOT BE USED FOR. It is a DIAGNOSTIC. The lift tables are computed on TEST-slice errors, so no feature may be defined from which hours they name -- that would be selection on test. A feature motivated by this must take its definition from the PUBLISHED RELEASE TIMES (8:30, 9:30 and 14:00 Eastern), which are structural facts about the schedule rather than anything fitted, and it needs its own pre-registration.
experiments.result: pre-registered, not yet run
experiments.implication:
EXPECTED OUTCOME, RECORDED BEFORE THE RUN. I expect the Eastern clock to concentrate the worst 5% more than UTC, and no fixed offset to beat it. If that holds, the reason a 23-column hour-of-day basis could not pay for itself at H=1 and H=6 becomes concrete: the model was being asked to learn each event TWICE, once per DST regime, in bins that are half empty each -- which doubles the parameters needed and halves the evidence per parameter. That is a specification error in the feature, not an absence of signal, and it is fixable with a single correctly-aligned column.
IF SOME FIXED OFFSET BEATS EASTERN, my reading is wrong and the doublets are an artifact of where the peak falls relative to hour boundaries. The honest conclusion would then be that the footprint is a UTC-anchored feature of crypto trading itself -- funding settlements at 00:00/08:00/16:00 UTC are the obvious candidate -- and the event story would be wrong.
IF NEITHER CLOCK SHOWS STRUCTURE AT H=1 the artifact disagrees with P2-event-footprint and something is wrong with this measurement rather than with the hypothesis.

experiments.question: Is the intraday error footprint sharper in US EASTERN local time than in UTC?
experiments.rule: As pre-registered -- except that the pre-registered control turned out to be incapable of returning another answer, which is reported below rather than quietly replaced.
experiments.result:
SUGGESTIVE AND NOT ESTABLISHED, AND THE PRE-REGISTERED CONTROL WAS VACUOUS.
H=1, 49,123 episodes, worst 5% = 2,457:
  UTC               chi2 324.7  p 4.5e-55  top-3 share 19.94%  14h(1.79) 18h(1.53) 19h(1.47)
  America/New_York  chi2 377.2  p 8.4e-66  top-3 share 21.29%  10h(1.80) 14h(1.75) 09h(1.56)
  chance level                              12.50%
The Eastern top-three hours are coherent with the schedule: 09h ET is the 9:30 cash open, 14h ET is the 2:00pm FOMC statement, 10h ET is the 10:00 release slot (ISM, confidence, etc.).
THE PRE-REGISTERED CONTROL CANNOT FAIL AND IS WITHDRAWN AS EVIDENCE. It compared Eastern against all 23 FIXED hour offsets. A fixed offset is a pure RELABELLING of 24 bins, so the bin counts are a permutation of themselves and chi-square, every lift and the top-K concentration are IDENTICAL to UTC by construction -- measured at 19.94% for all 23, invariant to 1e-12. My stated reasoning for the control ('a fixed offset moves both halves of a doublet together and can never merge them') was correct and is exactly why the control carries no information. That is R2, in the control I wrote to keep myself honest.
THE REPLACEMENT CONTROL, AND IT IS POST-HOC AND LABELLED SO. Placebo schedules with the SAME two offsets and the SAME two-transitions-a-year structure, transition dates moved by d days, d in +-7..175 in 7-day steps, 50 of them. Real schedule 21.29%; placebo mean 19.25%, sd 1.00pp, max 21.33%. z = +2.04, RANK 3 OF 51, empirical p about 0.06.
AND THE TWO PLACEBOS THAT BEAT IT ARE NOT INDEPENDENT OF IT: they are shifts of -7 and -14 days, which reclassify roughly 2-4% of days relative to the true schedule. They are the same clock with a smudge, not alternative hypotheses. Excluding |d| < 28 would put the real schedule first -- and that exclusion is chosen after seeing the result, so it is stated and not used.
H=24 CONTROL BEHAVES: chi-square 2.8 in Eastern against 3.0 in UTC, p = 1.000 for both, concentration 13.15% against a 12.50% chance level, and the real schedule ranks 37 of 51 among placebos (z = -0.22). No clock finds structure where P2-event-footprint established there is none.
experiments.implication:
THE PRE-REGISTERED VERDICT RULE CANNOT BE APPLIED, because it was conditioned on a control that has no power. What is left is an effect in the predicted direction with an empirical p of about 0.06 against a placebo family whose nearest members are near-duplicates of the truth. That is a reason to run a better test, not a result.
THE BETTER TEST IS OBVIOUS AND NEEDS NO NEW DATA. Stop measuring concentration and test the MECHANISM directly: split the episodes into US SUMMER and US WINTER and compare the two UTC lift tables. If scheduled Eastern-time releases drive the footprint, the summer peak must sit EXACTLY ONE HOUR EARLIER IN UTC than the winter peak. That is a point prediction about a specific integer, it has no tuning parameter, no concentration statistic and no placebo family, and it is falsified by any other offset including zero. It gets its own pre-registration.
WHAT THIS DOES NOT CHANGE. P2-event-footprint's finding stands untouched -- the H=1 footprint is real at chi-square 324.7 in UTC and 377.2 in Eastern, and flat at H=24 in both. The open question is only whether its ALIGNMENT is the US schedule, which decides whether a one-parameter event feature should be defined in Eastern local time or in UTC.
