(3) shrunk: beta = 1 + w(beta_hat - 1) with w = tau^2/(tau^2 + SE^2) -- SE the moving-block bootstrap error of that fold's own slope on its calib slice, tau^2 the between-fold variance of the TRUE slope estimated from PAST FOLDS ONLY as var(beta_hat) - mean(SE^2) floored at zero. (4) drift: the same form with SE^2 + D^2 in the denominator, where D^2 is the mean squared CALIB-to-TEST slope movement observed on PAST folds only. (5) half: a FIXED w = 0.5 at every horizon and fold -- the control. Walk-forward throughout: the first fold has no past, so it gets w = 0 and the level-only correction. Family fixed at 4 horizons x 6 contrasts ({shrunk, drift} x {c, mzq, half}) = 24, Bonferroni. The CLAIM being tested is non-inferiority: a rule succeeds only if it is not significantly worse than the better of c and mzq at EVERY horizon.
experiments.result: pre-registered before the run. PREDICTION, AND IT IS AGAINST MY OWN PRINCIPLED ARM. From the already-measured quantities, tau is roughly 0.198 / 0.199 / 0.219 / 0.328 and the mean calib SE is 0.029 / 0.050 / 0.085 / 0.150, so w = tau^2/(tau^2+SE^2) comes out near 0.98 / 0.94 / 0.87 / 0.83. The `shrunk` arm therefore barely shrinks ANYWHERE, including at H=168 where shrinkage is most needed, and I expect it to be indistinguishable from `mzq` at all four horizons and to remain far worse than `c` at H=168. The reason is a mis-targeted variance: empirical-Bayes asks how precisely a fold's slope is ESTIMATED, and at H=168 the slopes genuinely differ between folds (large tau), so the rule concludes the fold-specific slope is worth keeping. But the failure is not imprecision -- it is that a calib-fitted slope does not TRANSFER to that fold's own test slice, which is why 2022's calib slope of -0.017 sits beside its own test slope of 0.918. SPECIFIC AND UNCOMFORTABLE: I expect the arbitrary constant `half` to BEAT the principled `shrunk` at H=168, because 0.5 shrinks harder than 0.83 does. And I expect `drift`, which adds the measured calib-to-test movement to the denominator, to be the only arm that is never significantly worse than the better of c and mzq -- that is the claim, and if it fails the whole shrinkage framing is wrong rather than merely mis-parameterised. Confidence MODERATE on drift, HIGH on shrunk being a near-no-op.
experiments.notes: WHY THIS AND NOT A THRESHOLD. The obvious fix is 'use the slope below some horizon and drop it above'. That threshold would be fitted on the same four numbers that motivate the experiment, which is tuning to answers already seen; every arm here derives its behaviour from a quantity measured on past folds and none of them knows what a horizon is. WHY THE `half` CONTROL IS THE EXPERIMENT: if an arbitrary constant matches or beats the precision-weighted rule, then the measured standard errors contribute nothing and what works is shrinkage-in-general, not this shrinkage -- the same role the width-matched band played in P3-frvp-double-touch, where the placebo beat the real feature. NO RETRAINING: every arm is a post-hoc map on existing out-of-fold predictions, so this costs one pass over teacher_oof.npz and changes no model. WHAT IT WOULD MEAN IF `drift` WINS: the correction to adopt is horizon-free and self-tuning, and the H=168 result stops being a hole in the scorecard. WHAT IT WOULD MEAN IF NOTHING WINS: the slope is not recoverable by reweighting at all, and the honest move is to drop it at long horizons and say so, rather than to keep searching for a weighting that rescues it.

experiments.question: Closing P3-shrunk-slope. Can one rule, with no horizon-specific tuning, match the better of {level-only, full-slope} at every horizon?
experiments.rule: As pre-registered: five arms fitted on calib and applied to test, level re-optimised at each arm's slope; family 24 (4 horizons x {shrunk, drift} x {c, mzq, half}), Bonferroni to 99.79%; success is NON-INFERIORITY to the better of c and mzq at EVERY horizon.
experiments.result: THE CLAIM IS MET BY `drift` AND FAILED BY `shrunk`, AND THE CONTROL BEATS BOTH. Pooled QLIKE, c / mzq / shrunk / drift / half: H=1 0.54815 / 0.53295 / 0.54060 / 0.53481 / 0.52697; H=6 0.34715 / 0.33890 / 0.34290 / 0.33990 / 0.33509; H=24 0.24825 / 0.25159 / 0.24915 / 0.24822 / 0.24651; H=168 0.18565 / 0.22195 / 0.19967 / 0.18554 / 0.18800. `drift` is non-inferior to the better of {c, mzq} at all four horizons (-0.35% / -0.29% / +0.01% / +0.06%, every interval containing zero) and RECOVERS H=168 completely -- 0.18554 against mzq's 0.22195, worth +16.41%, and marginally the best arm at that horizon. `shrunk` FAILS the claim: significantly worse than mzq at H=1, CI [-0.01651, -0.00088]. BUT THE ARBITRARY CONSTANT IS THE BEST ARM AT THREE OF FOUR HORIZONS and beats BOTH principled rules with intervals excluding zero at H=1 and H=6.
experiments.notes: PREDICTION SCORING, MIXED. CORRECT: `drift` would be the only arm never significantly worse than the better of c and mzq -- it is, and `shrunk` is not. CORRECT IN DIRECTION: `half` would beat `shrunk` at H=168 (0.18800 against 0.19967), though the interval contains zero. WRONG: I predicted `shrunk` would be INDISTINGUISHABLE from mzq everywhere; it is significantly WORSE at H=1. NOT PREDICTED AT ALL: that the control would dominate at the SHORT horizons. I registered `half` as a control expected to expose a mis-parameterised candidate at H=168, and it instead won at H=1, H=6 and H=24. THE MECHANISM, DIAGNOSED RATHER THAN ASSUMED, AND IT EXONERATES THE WEIGHTING. `drift`'s fitted weights on folds that HAVE a past are 0.535/0.535/0.548/0.533 at H=1, 0.543/0.527/0.535/0.517 at H=6, 0.556/0.503/0.477/0.451 at H=24 and 0.505/0.428/0.398/0.345 at H=168. It DERIVES approximately one half at the short horizons -- the control's constant, recovered from measured variances rather than assumed -- and shrinks progressively harder as the horizon lengthens, which is precisely the horizon-adaptive behaviour the experiment was built to obtain, and is why it is the only arm that fixes H=168. Its entire deficit against the constant is a COLD START: tau^2 needs two past folds, so 2021 and 2022 get w = 0 and are scored with no slope correction at all. A third of the sample runs on the wrong arm. So the honest reading is NOT 'the arbitrary constant beats the measured rule' but 'the measured rule reproduces the constant where the constant is right, improves on it where it is wrong, and loses on a start-up policy that was never the object of study'. THAT IS A TESTABLE FIX rather than an excuse, and it is pre-registered separately (P3-warm-start) as: give the cold-start folds the fixed constant instead of w = 0, predict drift-with-warm-start matches or beats `half` at every horizon. NOT ADOPTED, AND `half` IS NOT PROMOTED: it entered this family as a CONTROL, and promoting a control to a candidate after seeing it win is family expansion after the fact -- the same defect R77 names. Any adoption needs its own registration.

experiments.question: P3-shrunk-slope-result diagnosed the drift rule's entire deficit against the fixed constant as a COLD START -- tau^2 needs two past folds, so 2021 and 2022 received w=0 and a third of the sample was scored with no slope correction. Does falling back to the constant until a real estimate exists close the gap?
experiments.rule: PRE-REGISTERED BEFORE THE RUN. One new arm, `drift_ws`, identical to `drift` in every respect except the start-up policy: where tau^2 cannot yet be formed it uses w = COLD_START_W instead of w = 0. COLD_START_W is set to exactly FIXED_W = 0.5, the control's own constant, so the fallback cannot be accused of being tuned -- it is the value that was already fixed a priori as the control. Nothing else changes: same folds, same calib fits, same level re-optimisation, same teacher. Family grows to 4 horizons x 3 candidates x 3 references = 36, Bonferroni to 99.861%, and the earlier arms are re-scored under the wider correction rather than keeping their old intervals. Success is the same non-inferiority claim as before, now against `half` as well: `drift_ws` must not be significantly worse than the better of {c, mzq, half} at ANY horizon.
experiments.result: pre-registered before the run. PREDICTION: `drift_ws` matches `half` at H=1, H=6 and H=24 -- because on the warm folds it already derives 0.535/0.535/0.548/0.533 and 0.543/0.527/0.535/0.517, within a few points of 0.5, so once the cold folds stop being handicapped there is nothing left to separate them -- and BEATS `half` at H=168, where its warm weights fall to 0.505/0.428/0.398/0.345 and the constant is too gentle (half 0.18800 against drift 0.18554 there already, with the cold-start handicap still in place). So I expect `drift_ws` to be the only arm that is never significantly worse than the best of the three references at all four horizons, and to be the outright best arm at H=168. Confidence MODERATE-HIGH on the short horizons because the mechanism is measured rather than hypothesised; LOWER on H=168 beating `half` with an interval that excludes zero, since n is smallest there and the two arms already sit within 1.3% of each other. FALSIFICATION THAT WOULD MATTER MOST: if `drift_ws` still loses to `half` at a short horizon, then the cold start was not the mechanism and the diagnosis in P3-shrunk-slope-result is wrong -- in which case the measured variances really are contributing nothing and a fixed constant is the honest recommendation.
experiments.notes: WHY THIS IS NOT POST-HOC TUNING, stated plainly because it is the obvious objection. The cold-start policy was never the object of the original experiment; it was an incidental choice made while writing the rule, and w = 0 was chosen because 'no estimate' felt like the conservative default. The diagnosis did not come from scanning parameters for a better score -- it came from printing the per-fold weights and noticing that the warm ones already reproduce the constant, so the only place the arms can differ is where the weight is not warm. The replacement value is not searched over: it is the control's constant, fixed before any of this ran. WHAT IS STILL NOT SETTLED EITHER WAY: `half` remains a CONTROL and is not promoted to a candidate here. If `drift_ws` merely ties it everywhere, the correct conclusion is that the measured variances buy nothing at these horizons and a fixed shrinkage is what should be registered for adoption -- separately, with its own family.

experiments.question: Closing P3-warm-start. Does falling back to the fixed constant on cold-start folds close drift's gap against it -- and does the measured-variance machinery then earn its keep?
experiments.rule: As pre-registered: `drift_ws` identical to `drift` except that folds without a formable tau^2 use w = 0.5 instead of w = 0. Family 36 (4 horizons x 3 candidates x 3 references), Bonferroni to 99.861%, all earlier arms re-scored under the wider correction. Success is non-inferiority to the best of {c, mzq, half} at every horizon.
experiments.result: THE CLAIM IS MET AND THE MACHINERY IS STILL NOT JUSTIFIED. Pooled QLIKE, c / mzq / shrunk / drift / drift_ws / half: H=1 0.54815 / 0.53295 / 0.54060 / 0.53481 / 0.52672 / 0.52697; H=6 0.34715 / 0.33890 / 0.34290 / 0.33990 / 0.33496 / 0.33509; H=24 0.24825 / 0.25159 / 0.24915 / 0.24822 / 0.24655 / 0.24651; H=168 0.18565 / 0.22195 / 0.19967 / 0.18554 / 0.18670 / 0.18800. `drift_ws` is non-inferior to the best reference at all four horizons (+0.05% / +0.04% / -0.02% / -0.56%, every interval containing zero) and is the outright best arm at H=1 and H=6. THE COLD START WAS THE MECHANISM, as diagnosed: warm-starting moves H=1 from 0.53481 to 0.52672 and H=6 from 0.33990 to 0.33496, exactly the two horizons where the handicap cost most. BUT THE HEAD-TO-HEAD IS NOT SEPARATED AT ANY HORIZON, with intervals as tight as [-0.00016, +0.00061] at H=1. A fixed one-half is statistically indistinguishable from a rule that bootstraps a standard error per fold, estimates a between-fold variance from past folds, measures calib-to-test drift, and combines the three. The measured variances buy nothing.
experiments.notes: PREDICTION SCORING. CORRECT: `drift_ws` matches `half` at H=1, H=6 and H=24 -- not separated at all three, point estimates within 0.05%. WRONG: I predicted it would BEAT `half` at H=168 with an interval excluding zero. It is better by point estimate (0.18670 against 0.18800, +0.69%) and the interval contains zero. WORSE THAN THAT, AND UNPREDICTED: warm-starting made H=168 slightly worse than plain `drift` (0.18670 against 0.18554), because at that horizon w = 0 -- the level-only correction -- is very nearly the right answer, so the cold-start policy I called a handicap was accidentally correct there. A fix aimed at one horizon's mechanism cost a little at another, which is the ordinary shape of a change made for a good reason. THE THIRD TIME THIS HAS HAPPENED. A permuted column outscored every explicit regulariser (P3-regularisation-result); a width-matched band centred where the volume profile did not point matched or beat the real flag at all twelve settings (P3-frvp-sensitivity); a fixed constant now matches an empirical-Bayes rule with three measured variance components at all four horizons. Three different subsystems, same lesson, recorded as R82. WHAT IS INDICATED AND WHAT IS NOT. A fixed 50% slope shrinkage is the rule to carry forward: it beats the better of {c, mzq} by +1.12% / +1.12% / +0.70% at H = 1 / 6 / 24 and loses 1.27% at H=168. It is NOT adopted here. `half` entered as a control and has now been looked at across two runs on the same out-of-fold set, so its margin is no longer a clean out-of-sample estimate -- promoting it on this evidence is the family expansion R77 names, one step removed. The confirmatory evaluation belongs on the untouched 2026-08-28 forward holdout, which gets exactly one evaluation (R26) and should not be spent until there is a full candidate configuration worth spending it on.
